articles.name: Lest We Forget the Horrors: An Unending Catalog of Trump’s Cruelties, Collusions, Corruptions, and Crimes: May 2026: Atrocities 931-1013
articles.author: Emily Greenberg and Chase Bush-McLaughlin
articles.full_text:
Early in President Trump’s first term, McSweeney’s editors began to catalog the head-spinning number of misdeeds coming from his administration. We called this list a collection of Trump’s cruelties, collusions, corruptions, and crimes, and it felt urgent to track them, to ensure these horrors—happening almost daily—would not be forgotten. Now that Trump has returned to office, amid civil rights, humanitarian, economic, and constitutional crises, we felt it critical to make an inventory of this new round of horrors. This list will be updated monthly between now and the end of Donald Trump’s second term.
These lists, along with everything McSweeney’s publishes on this site, are offered ad-free and at no charge to our readers. If you are moved to make a donation in any amount or subscribe to our website’s Patreon, please do. This will help support this project and our other work.
ATROCITY KEY
 – Authoritarianism 
 – Constitutional Illegalities, Collusion, and/or Obstruction of Justice
 – Environment
 – Harassment, Bullying, Retribution, and/or Sexual Misconduct
 – Lies and Misinformation
 – Musk Madness
 – Policy
 – Public Statements and Social Media Posts
 – Trump Family Business Dealings
 – Trump Staff and Administration
 – White Supremacy, Racism, Misogyny, Homophobia, Transphobia, and/or Xenophobia
April 2026
Main Index
Trump’s first term
May 2026
- – May 1, 2026 – In the months since Congress let Obamacare subsidies expire, many have dropped their health care coverage. Enrollment fell by 1.2 million, and insurers estimated that approximately 5 million had lost their coverage. The Wakely Consulting Group estimated that marketplace coverage would fall by 26 percent this year compared to last year. Despite the massive coverage losses, Trump administration officials continued to paint a rosy view. “The marketplace remains strong and resilient, continuing to provide millions of Americans with access to high-quality, affordable health care coverage options,” said Chris Krepich, an official with the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.
 
 
- – May 1, 2026 – Making good on Trump’s earlier threat, the Pentagon announced it would withdraw five thousand troops from Germany in the next year, with Trump promising further withdrawals. The announcement came several days after German Chancellor Friedrich Merz criticized the war in Iran. Republican chairs of the House and Senate Armed Services committees said they were “very concerned.”
 
 
- – May 1, 2026 – Trump mocked a transgender weightlifter in a speech delivered to a Florida retirement community. After performing an impression of the weightlifter, Trump admitted that the first lady had asked him not to do it. “She hates it when I do the thing on weightlifting,” Trump said. “She says it’s so unpresidential.”
 
 
 Donald Trump Seen Mocking and Mimicking Transgender Weightlifters (News18)
 
 
- – May 1, 2026 – Construction to expand Trump’s border wall bulldozed an ancient tribal site in the Arizona desert. Ignoring environmental laws and other protections, the construction crew damaged a more than two-hundred-foot-long ground etching resembling a fish that was thought to be at least one thousand years old. “There are very few intaglios in this area, so by losing part of it, it’s a big deal,” said Sandra Martynec, an archaeologist who discovered the intaglio in archaeological surveys of the area along with her husband, Richard Martynec, also an archaeologist. “Those things were made by our ancestors, and it’s hitting home.… For me, it’s an emotional subject,” added Lorraine Marquez Eiler, an elder of the Hia C-ed O’odham Indigenous people.
 
 
- – May 1, 2026 – In its push to create a national directory of health care providers, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services exposed providers’ Social Security numbers and other identifying information. The information was publicly available for several weeks. “The more we learn about how the Trump administration handles the people’s most sensitive data, the clearer their incompetence becomes,” said Democratic Representative Richard E. Neal, who called on Republicans to launch an investigation.
 
 
- – May 1, 2026 – Trump posted multiple AI-generated photos to Truth Social, including an image of himself, his face visibly superimposed onto a more muscular body, floating shirtless in the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool with Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, and an unidentified bikini-clad woman. In another post, Trump shared a photo of House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is Black, and called Jeffries “low IQ” and a “thug.”
 
 
 
 
- – May 3, 2026 – Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche defended the Trump administration’s prosecution of former FBI Director James Comey. Comey had posted a photo of seashells spelling out “86 47,” a phrase prosecutors characterized as a threat to remove or kill the forty-seventh president. Blanche conceded that the phrase was “posted constantly” and said, “Every one of those statements do not result in indictments.” He declined to describe the additional evidence that made Comey’s case different.
 
 
- – May 4, 2026 – The Trump administration ordered federal lands across the country to eliminate dozens of hunting and trapping restrictions designed to protect visitors, habitats, and wildlife. Critics said the move appeared to violate the National Park Service’s duty under the 1916 Organic Act to conserve park resources “unimpaired” for future generations. The memo directing the changes did not call for analysis, public engagement, or review of whether the rollbacks would leave parks unimpaired, while the rules targeted for repeal included restrictions on firing weapons near trails, leaving animal carcasses, and cleaning game animals in public restrooms.
 
 
- – May 4, 2026 – The Department of Homeland Security publicly attacked a federal judge for releasing an immigrant detainee whom the agency later said was wanted for homicide in the Dominican Republic. Government lawyer Kevin Bolan later revealed that ICE had instructed him not to disclose the overseas charge to the court before the hearing, even as the administration subsequently publicized the same allegation to attack the judge’s ruling. Calling the episode “a serious breakdown in the ethical codes,” Judge Melissa DuBose said there had been “a decision made not to be truthful to the court.” Internal emails later showed that an ICE lawyer had explicitly directed Bolan to “not confirm or deny the existence” of the warrant.
 
 
- – May 4, 2026 – Fulton County, Georgia, revealed in a court filing that the Justice Department had subpoenaed the names, positions, email addresses, and personal phone numbers of thousands of people who helped administer the county’s 2020 election. The county moved to block the subpoena, arguing that its purpose was to “target, harass, and punish” Trump’s perceived political opponents. The filing noted that Trump had “obsessively propagated the debunked conspiracy theory that Fulton County ‘stole’ the 2020 election from him” and had called for Ruby Freeman and top Georgia officials to be prosecuted for “the political crime of the century.” Two days later, a federal judge declined to order the return of roughly 660 boxes of 2020 election records seized by the FBI from Fulton County in January, allowing the Justice Department to retain ballots, voter rolls, and scanner images while its investigation continued. The judge described aspects of the case as “troubling” and “unprecedented” but ruled that the county had not shown the government acted with “callous disregard” for its constitutional rights.
 
 
- – May 4, 2026 – Senate Republicans released an immigration-enforcement bill that included $1 billion for security upgrades tied to Trump’s East Wing renovation. The money was added to a roughly $70 billion package for ICE, border patrol, and related enforcement spending, even though Republicans had sought to keep the bill limited to immigration measures so it could move quickly before Trump’s June 1 deadline. The funding could help clear legal obstacles to Trump’s planned ballroom, which a federal judge had ruled required congressional approval, despite Trump’s earlier claim that the project would be privately funded.
 
 
- – May 4, 2026 – At a Small Business Week event the White House billed as “the extraordinary revival of Main Street under his America First agenda,” Trump said tax and regulation cuts had produced “record business” and declared that the economy was “roaring.” At the time, gas prices had risen by more than a dollar per gallon from the previous year, diesel prices were up by roughly two dollars per gallon, and debt held by the public had surpassed the size of the entire US economy for the first time since World War II. The Congressional Budget Office projected that Trump’s tax package would add trillions to federal deficits while increasing interest costs by another $551 billion over the next decade.
 
 
- – May 5, 2026 – Trump paused Project Freedom, the US mission to guide commercial ships through the Strait of Hormuz, a day after announcing it. The reversal came hours after Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended the mission, saying Iran’s control of the waterway was “completely illegal, completely illegitimate, and completely unacceptable” and that the US military was “putting an end to these efforts to hold the global economy hostage.” Before Trump suspended the operation, only three ships had made the passage under US military protection, compared to roughly 130 vessels a day before the war, while roughly 1,600 vessels remained stranded.
 
 
- – May 5, 2026 – Palm Beach County approved a licensing agreement with the Trump Organization to use the name “President Donald J. Trump International Airport,” clearing the way for the renaming of Palm Beach International Airport. The Trump Organization had previously trademarked the airport name, along with the proposed airport code “DJT,” and sought trademark protection for related merchandise. While the agreement barred the Trump family from profiting off merchandise sold at the airport itself, it did not prevent the company from profiting from such merchandise sold elsewhere. The deal also gave the Trump Organization control over biographical material presented at the airport and required officials to select merchandise vendors from a list approved by the company. A trademark lawyer described the arrangement as “extremely unusual.”
 
 
- – May 5, 2026 – The White House marked Cinco de Mayo by posting an AI-generated image of House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer wearing sombreros at the US-Mexico border. The two were depicted drinking margaritas beside tortilla chips, dip, a potted cactus, and a sign reading, “I LOVE ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS.” The image was captioned, “Happy Cinco de Mayo to all who celebrate!” It echoed a 2025 Trump video that depicted Jeffries with a fake mustache and sombrero while mariachi music played in the background. At the time, Vice President JD Vance had joked that “the sombrero memes will stop” if Jeffries helped Republicans reopen the government.
 
 
- – May 6, 2026 – The White House released a new national counterterrorism strategy drafted by adviser Sebastian Gorka that omitted far-right extremism entirely. The strategy instead elevated “violent leftists” to a threat on par with foreign terrorist organizations, despite federal authorities having for years identified white-supremacist and other racially motivated extremists as among the country’s most active and lethal domestic terrorist threats. The document described Christians as “the most persecuted people on Earth” and called for the “neutralization of violent secular political groups whose ideology is anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist.”
 
 
- – May 6, 2026 – Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick spent hours before the House Oversight Committee defending his ties to Jeffrey Epstein after Justice Department records contradicted his previous public statements. Lutnick had said in 2025 that after an uncomfortable encounter with Epstein in 2005, he was never again “in the room” with him socially, professionally, or philanthropically. But records released from the Epstein files showed that Lutnick and his family visited Epstein’s private island in 2012, four years after Epstein pleaded guilty to soliciting prostitution from a minor, and continued to have other contacts with him. House Oversight Committee chair James Comer acknowledged that Lutnick “wasn’t 100 percent truthful” about whether he had been on the island. Weeks later, campaign finance filings revealed that Lutnick had donated $5 million to a super PAC backing House Republicans after agreeing to testify before the committee and before his May 6 appearance.
 
 
- – May 7, 2026 – ProPublica found that at least seventy-nine children had been harmed by tear gas or pepper spray during Trump’s immigration crackdown, including children exposed while walking to school, sitting in cars, and sheltering inside their homes. Federal judges in multiple cities had described ICE and Customs and Border Protection officers’ use of chemical weapons as excessive, with one judge writing that “tear-gassing expectant mothers, children, and babies shocks the conscience.” The Department of Homeland Security defended its agents, laying the blame on “agitators” and parents who brought children into dangerous situations.
 
 
- – May 7, 2026 – A White House panel appointed by Trump recommended overhauling FEMA by shifting more disaster costs and responsibilities to states, limiting the agency’s role in long-term recovery and housing assistance, and privatizing the National Flood Insurance Program. The panel rejected Trump’s earlier suggestion that FEMA should “go away” altogether but argued that federal disaster aid should be reserved for “truly significant events” and that states had become too reliant on federal funding. The recommendations came as forecasters warned that a developing El Niño could increase the risk of extreme weather in the months ahead.
 
 
- – May 7, 2026 – Tennessee Republicans approved a new congressional map designed to eliminate the state’s last Democratic House seat by splitting majority-Black Memphis among three districts. Governor Bill Lee signed the map after a special session he called at Trump’s urging, part of a broader Republican redistricting push ahead of the midterms. The map was the first enacted after the Supreme Court weakened what remained of the Voting Rights Act’s protections against racial gerrymandering; State Representative Jason Zachary said the goal was an all-Republican delegation: “We’re taking advantage of that as the supermajority in this body.”
 
 
 Tennessee Democrats Lock Arms in Protest as State Lawmakers Vote for New Congressional Map (PBS News Hour)
 
 
- – May 7, 2026 – The Trump administration lifted a ban on the use of “cyanide bombs” on public lands managed by the Bureau of Land Management. The devices, also known as M-44s, spray a lethal dose of sodium cyanide when triggered and are used to kill coyotes, foxes, and other predators that threaten livestock. The Biden administration had banned them in 2023 over safety concerns, citing several incidents in which the devices harmed people and pets. In one 2017 incident in Idaho, an M-44 placed on public land four hundred feet from a family’s home killed their dog and temporarily blinded a fourteen-year-old boy.
 
 
- – May 7, 2026 – Trump pushed to have the historic Eisenhower Executive Office Building painted white so it would better match the White House and his planned ballroom. Painting, cleaning, and preserving the granite building, which was constructed between 1871 and 1888 and houses hundreds of federal workers, would cost an estimated $7.5 million. During a public comment period, the proposal drew overwhelmingly negative feedback, including from Margo Steinberg, a historic preservation official who called it “an absolute disgrace” and “such a stupid idea.” Trump had previously displayed a rendering of the building on Fox News, saying, “Look at that, how beautiful that is with a coat of paint,” and adding that “gray is for funerals.”
 
 
- – May 7, 2026 – The Justice Department subpoenaed NYU Langone Health for information about patients under eighteen who received gender-affirming care between 2020 and 2026, as well as the names of medical staff members who provided it. The subpoena came from the US attorney’s office in the Northern District of Texas, even though NYU Langone is based in New York, where state law required the hospital to notify the attorney general before complying. Trump had previously signed an executive order describing transition care for minors as “maiming and sterilizing” children, and last year the FBI asked the public to report doctors who “mutilate” children “under the guise of gender-affirming care.”
 
 
- – May 8, 2026 – The Postal Service moved to allow handguns to be sent through the mail after Trump’s Justice Department declared a 1927 law restricting the practice unconstitutional. The proposal would let people ship unloaded, securely packaged handguns under the same rules that apply to rifles and shotguns. Attorneys general from twenty-one jurisdictions objected that the administration had no authority to set aside a law passed by Congress.
 
 
- – May 10, 2026 – The Washington Post reported that the US deported a twenty-eight-year-old woman who had fled genital mutilation in Togo to neighboring Ghana. Although a US judge had ruled that the Trump administration could not deport the woman to Togo, she was eventually taken there after spending two weeks in Ghana. The Post found that the Trump administration had also deported hundreds of others to countries they were not from in what are known as “third-country deportations.” “I know God is with me, but I’m tired. I’m a human being. I have to live, like everybody else,” said the woman, who was in hiding.
 
 
- – May 10, 2026 – Kevin Gonzalez, 18, died hours after seeing his parents, who were released just a day earlier from immigration custody. Earlier this year, Gonzalez was diagnosed with terminal colon cancer in Chicago, where he remained to receive treatment. When his parents crossed the border from Mexico to see him in mid-April, they were detained and moved to an immigration center in Arizona. Gonzalez subsequently went to live with his grandmother in Mexico as a legal battle unfolded to secure his parents’ release. After his parents were granted an expedited release on May 8, they raced to see their son, who died just hours after the family was reunited.
 
 
- – May 11, 2026 – The Wall Street Journal said it had received Department of Justice subpoenas on March 4 for its reporters’ records in connection with media leaks related to the Iran war. The subpoenas referred to a February 23 Journal article that stated General Dan Caine, chair of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and other Pentagon officials had warned Trump about the risks of war with Iran. The Journal’s parent company, Dow Jones, called the subpoenas “an attack on constitutionally protected newsgathering.”
 
 
- – May 11, 2026 – In a flurry of late-night Truth Social posts, Trump reposted several posts by other users baselessly accusing former President Barack Obama of treason and calling for his arrest. One post called Obama “the most DEMONIC FORCE in American politics in decades”; another said that Hillary Clinton should be deported to Haiti. Others made false claims about the 2020 election, called for other political opponents to be jailed, and attacked The New York Times.
 
 
- – May 12, 2026 – When asked whether Americans’ dire financial situations were motivating him to negotiate a deal with Iran, Trump responded, “Not even a little bit.”
 
 
 Trump Says He Does Not Consider American Financial Situations in Iran Talks (NBC News)
 
 
- – May 12, 2026 – Classified US intelligence assessments showed that Iran retained substantial missile capabilities, including operational access to thirty of its thirty-three missile sites along the Strait of Hormuz. The assessments contradicted multiple statements made by Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth about Iran’s military capabilities.
 
 
- – May 12, 2026 – A Washington Post investigation found that a large percentage of men deported under the Trump administration had lived in the US for years and did not have criminal records. Of the 300,000 men deported since Trump’s second term began, nearly a quarter had lived in the US for over three years, and nearly two-thirds had no criminal record. 
 
 
- – May 12, 2026 – Democratic Congressman Jamie Raskin claimed that the Justice Department had paid millions to Trump-allied FBI agents suspended for misconduct. One of the agents was suspended after refusing to investigate a white-nationalist group, and another for being present in a restricted area during the January 6, 2021, Capitol attack. “These checks are just political handouts and payoffs,” Raskin wrote in a letter to acting Attorney General Todd Blanche.
 
 
- – May 13, 2026 – Eric Trump accompanied his father on his trip to China. Although the Trump Organization claimed Trump’s middle son was only joining his father in a “personal capacity,” Eric Trump has reported owning dozens of trademarks in China that could allow him to earn money from future developments, and the Trump Organization has explored business deals with China in the past.
 
 
- – May 13, 2026 – Kevin Warsh was confirmed as Federal Reserve Board chair in a divisive 54–45 vote mostly along party lines. During Warsh’s confirmation hearings, he declined to answer whether Trump had lost the 2020 election. Democrats also raised concerns that Warsh, whose views on inflation have shifted to align more with Trump’s since he served on the Fed over a decade ago, would function as a “sock puppet” for Trump and compromise the Fed’s independence. Trump said he expected Warsh to lower interest rates despite growing inflation.
 
 
 Fed Chair Nom Kevin Warsh Refuses to Say Trump Lost 2020 Election When Asked by Warren (Forbes)
 
 
- – May 13, 2026 – The Trump administration announced it would withhold $1.3 billion in Medicaid payments to California, alleging that the state had failed to combat fraud in managing hospice care. The announcement followed a similar move in February to withhold $259 million in payments to Minnesota, also a Democrat-led state.
 
 
- – May 13, 2026 – A federal judge ordered the Trump administration to return Adriana Maria Quiroz Zapata, 55, a Colombian woman it had deported to the Congo, back to the US. Quiroz Zapata had fled Colombia to escape her former partner, who had ties to the Colombian police, and an immigration judge had ruled she could not be deported to her home country because she was likely to face violence. The Trump administration instead deported Quiroz Zapata to the Congo, even after the DRC refused to accept her due to her medical conditions. “There is no question that plaintiff meets the standard for irreparable harm. She has been sent to a country that refused to accept her because it cannot provide sufficient medical care. As a result, she faces a daily risk of medical complications, up to and including death,” wrote Judge Richard J. Leon.
 
 
- – May 14, 2026 – Admiral Brad Cooper, who oversaw US combat operations in Iran, dismissed reports of civilian deaths. Cooper said that the estimated 175 civilians killed in a February 28 bombing of an Iranian school were the only civilian casualties he knew about, despite multiple reports to the contrary. According to the Iranian Red Crescent Society, more than 763 schools and 316 medical facilities were damaged or destroyed as of April 2. The Human Rights Activists News Agency said at least 1,700 Iranian civilians had been killed as of mid-April.
 
 
- – May 14, 2026 – The EPA proposed ending a Biden-era rule preventing coal plants from polluting nearby waters. The 2024 rule required plants to filter toxic metals from their wastewater and was predicted to prevent an estimated 660 million pounds of pollutants each year. On the same day, the EPA also announced it would delay the implementation of a Biden-era air pollution limit for cars and trucks by two years. “An administration that claims to want to ‘Make America Healthy Again’ just made it easier for coal plants to poison our water,” said Patrick Drupp, the climate policy director of the Sierra Club.
 
 
- – May 15, 2026 – Two weeks after announcing it would withdraw five thousand troops from Germany, the Pentagon abruptly canceled the deployment of over four thousand troops to Poland. The canceled deployments came after European allies criticized the US war in Iran and were also part of the US’s broader plan to scale back after Trump demanded NATO take a larger role in defending Europe.
 
 
- – May 16, 2026 – ICE deported Wendy Hernandez Reyes, 29, without her two-year-old son Orlin and then blamed Reyes for Orlin’s killing, according to a Washington Post report. After Reyes and her sister were detained in January, Reyes pleaded with ICE officers to let her son go with her, but they refused. Orlin instead went to live with his uncle, Samuel Maldonado Erazo, in Florida. Police said Maldonado violently abused Orlin, eventually killing him in March. An autopsy revealed multiple broken bones and evidence of sexual battery, repeated blows, stomping, and burning. A week after Orlin died, acting ICE director Todd M. Lyons blamed Reyes for her son’s death, falsely claiming she “chose to leave her son here with a violent murderer who took his life.” “How could I abandon my son, if my son was the love of my life? I did everything with my son. I am not a bad mother who left my child with a killer,” said Reyes. 
 
 
- – May 17, 2026 – At a National Mall rally that Trump promoted as a chance to “rededicate America as one nation under God,” members of his administration pushed the claim that the United States was founded as an explicitly Christian nation. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth invoked an apocryphal story of George Washington praying at Valley Forge, urging the crowd to pray “as Washington did on that momentous day.” Trump also appeared via prerecorded video, reading from 2 Chronicles, in what appeared to be footage from an earlier “organized” marathon Bible reading by a Texas activist. House Speaker Mike Johnson closed by declaring, “We hereby rededicate the United States of America as one nation under God.” Pulitzer Prize–winning historian Joseph Ellis called the Christian-founding narrative “nonsensical” and “dead wrong.”
 
 
 Speaker of the House Mike Johnson Leads Prayer at “Rededicate 250” Event on National Mall (Forbes)
 
 
- – May 18, 2026 – The Justice Department announced the creation of a $1.8 billion “Anti-Weaponization Fund” to compensate people claiming they were victims of government “lawfare” or political targeting. The fund was established as part of a settlement in Trump’s lawsuit against the IRS over the leak of his tax returns. Trump, Donald Trump Jr., Eric Trump, and the Trump Organization agreed to drop the lawsuit in exchange for a formal apology and the creation of a fund that will distribute taxpayer money through a five-member commission appointed by Attorney General Todd Blanche. Potential recipients could include some of the nearly 1,600 January 6 defendants pardoned by Trump, as well as entities associated with Trump himself. The proposal later provoked bipartisan backlash and multiple legal challenges, while Trump and administration officials gave conflicting legal signals about whether it would ultimately move forward.
 
 
- – May 18, 2026 – The New York Times reported that the United States had spent months negotiating a new arrangement with Denmark and Greenland that would dramatically expand American influence over the Arctic island. According to officials familiar with the talks, the Trump administration was seeking the right to keep US troops in Greenland indefinitely, even if the island became independent, as well as effective veto power over major investment deals involving countries such as China and Russia. Greenlandic officials said the proposals would significantly constrain the island’s sovereignty, with one member of Parliament warning that, under such an arrangement, Greenlanders might as well raise their own flag “halfway.”
 
 
- – May 18, 2026 – Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth appeared at a Kentucky campaign rally for Ed Gallrein, the Republican primary challenger to Representative Thomas Massie, a frequent critic of Trump. Speaking in what he described as his “personal capacity,” Hegseth accused Massie of undermining fellow Republicans and urged voters to replace him. The appearance marked a rare intervention by a sitting defense secretary in a congressional primary and came amid a broader Trump-backed effort to unseat Massie, who had voted against Trump’s tax bill, criticized the war in Iran, opposed aid to Israel, and pushed to compel the release of the Epstein files.
 
 
- – May 18, 2026 – Minnesota prosecutors charged ICE agent Christian Castro with felony assault for shooting Venezuelan immigrant Julio Sosa-Celis during the Trump administration’s Operation Metro Surge immigration crackdown. Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem had initially described the incident as an “attempted murder” of a federal agent, but charges against Sosa-Celis were later dropped after video footage surfaced that contradicted agents’ claims of a prolonged attack. Castro was the second federal immigration agent charged by Minnesota prosecutors over conduct during the operation.
 
 
- – May 18, 2026 – Trump threatened a “full, large-scale assault of Iran” if a nuclear deal was not reached, then told reporters he had called off “a very major attack tomorrow,” saying “we’ve had very big discussions with Iran.” “I put it off for a little while, hopefully maybe forever, but possibly for a little while,” he said.
 
 
 Tehran Threatens to Open “New Fronts” Against US If Trump Launches Fresh Strikes (The Independent)
 
 
- – May 18, 2026 – The Trump administration announced plans to repeal federal drinking water limits on four “forever chemicals,” also called PFAS, which persist in the environment and build up in the body. The EPA had linked long-term PFAS exposure to kidney cancer, immune suppression, and developmental problems in infants and children. The agency said it would restart the rule-making process for those chemicals, delaying new limits for years, while giving water utilities more time to comply with restrictions on two others.
 
 
- – May 19, 2026 – The New York Times reported that David Schutzenhofer, the general manager of Trump’s Bedminster golf club, helped shape plans for the renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and recruited one of the contractors later awarded a $1.7 million no-bid federal contract. The Interior Department said Schutzenhofer was serving as an unpaid adviser rather than a temporary government employee, a status that would have required ethics training and a pledge to avoid conflicts of interest.
 
 
- – May 19, 2026 – Well into the third month of the war in Iran, Trump brought reporters to the White House to show off construction on his planned $400 million, 90,000-square-foot ballroom. He said he did not “really have enough time” to explain the war but described the ballroom’s Greek and Roman design influences, its planned six-story underground bunker, and its “impenetrable steel” and “impenetrable glass.” “I’m a really good builder,” Trump said. “The thing I do best in life is build.”
 
 
 Trump Shows Ballroom Construction Amid Funding Uncertainty (CNN)
 
 
- – May 20, 2026 – On the anniversary of Cuba’s formal independence in 1902, when the United States ended its military occupation of the island after securing broad intervention rights through the Platt Amendment, the Justice Department indicted former Cuban president Raúl Castro on murder and conspiracy charges related to the 1996 downing of two civilian aircraft, which killed four people, including three Americans. The announcement came amid an escalating Trump administration pressure campaign against Cuba that has included an effective oil blockade and repeated suggestions of regime change. The same day, the comptroller general of the Republic of Cuba released an article characterizing May 20, 1902, as the birth of “a neocolony of the nascent, turbulent, and brutal Northern empire that despises us.” Cuba’s UN ambassador, Ernesto Soberón Guzmán, said Havana remained willing to negotiate with the United States but accused the administration of undermining diplomacy through “warmongering rhetoric” and “building different pretexts for military aggression against Cuba.”
 
 
- – May 20, 2026 – The World Health Organization projected that the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Uganda involved nearly six hundred suspected cases and 139 suspected deaths, warning that the numbers were likely to rise. Public health experts and aid workers said the response had been hampered by the Trump administration’s dismantling of USAID and cuts at the CDC, which had previously supported disease surveillance and emergency response across the region. American officials learned of the outbreak nine days after the WHO and nearly a month after the first known death.
 
 
- – May 20, 2026 – Campaign finance filings revealed that a Reynolds American subsidiary donated $5 million to Trump’s MAGA Inc. super PAC on April 30. Within the next two weeks, Reynolds executives and lobbyists met with Trump to complain about FDA regulation of e-cigarettes, the FDA adopted new guidance opening a path for major tobacco companies to market flavored vapes, and FDA Commissioner Marty Makary resigned after telling associates he would not approve a policy that could attract young people to vaping.
 
 
- – May 21, 2026 – Trump announced that his administration would delay the phaseout of hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), powerful greenhouse gases used in refrigeration and air conditioning, despite having signed the bipartisan law requiring their reduction during his first term. The administration claimed the move would lower grocery prices, though economists said any effect would likely be negligible. According to the EPA, a global phaseout of HFCs could avert up to 0.5 degrees Celsius of warming by the end of the century.
 
 
- – May 21, 2026 – A federal appeals court declined to review Mahmoud Khalil’s challenge to his deportation proceedings, potentially clearing the way for his deportation. Earlier that month, The Intercept reported that newly released FBI records showed the bureau had closed an investigation into an anonymous tip accusing Khalil of calling for “violence on behalf of Hamas.” The FBI concluded that Khalil “does not warrant further FBI investigation,” even as the Trump administration continued portraying him as a national security threat.
 
 
- – May 22, 2026 – The Trump administration announced that immigrants seeking green cards could be required to leave the United States and apply from abroad, raising fears of prolonged family separations and disruptions for employers. After widespread confusion and backlash, the Department of Homeland Security appeared to walk back the announcement, saying the policy would not apply broadly and would instead be left to the discretion of individual immigration officers.
 
 
- – May 22, 2026 – Tulsi Gabbard submitted her letter of resignation as director of national intelligence, effective June 30, becoming the fourth woman to leave Trump’s cabinet. During her time in office, Gabbard sparked controversy when she appeared at an FBI raid to seize ballots from the 2020 election, called for the investigation of Barack Obama and several of his former national security officials, revoked security clearances for career intelligence officers, and released previously classified files about the assassinations of John F. Kennedy, Robert F. Kennedy, and Martin Luther King Jr. Although Gabbard cited her husband’s recent cancer diagnosis as the reason for her resignation, she was reportedly forced out after being sidelined on operations in Iran and Venezuela. Trump had previously said he didn’t care what Gabbard said about Iran and called her statement that Iran was not building a nuclear weapon “wrong.”
 
 
- – May 22, 2026 – The Trump administration narrowed the definition of “assistance animal” in housing, telling HUD fair-housing officials to exclude emotional support animals and more strictly limit accommodations to trained service animals. The change reversed guidance from Trump’s first term and could affect disabled tenants who rely on animals for psychiatric or mental health conditions, including veterans with PTSD.
 
 
- – May 25, 2026 – Left without cooking gas due to the US oil blockade, millions in Cuba have been forced to cook with charcoal and wood. “I shouldn’t be cooking with charcoal. But if I don’t cook, I die,” said Yusimi Castellano, 58, who has asthma.
 
 
- – May 25, 2026 – Democratic Senator Andy Kim was pepper-sprayed, along with numerous other protesters, during a demonstration against ICE. “What we saw here is unfortunately just what we see all over the country. It’s sad; it’s a sad day,” said Kim. DHS claimed no one was “directly struck by pepper ball projectiles,” though Kim described being struck in the head by an unknown object and inhaling chemical irritants. Kim and the other protestors were responding to an inmate hunger strike over inhumane conditions at Delaney Hall, a privately run immigration detention center in Newark. Multiple Democratic officials have called for Delaney Hall to be shut down. 
 
 
 US Sen. Andy Kim Pepper-Sprayed During Protests at Newark Detention Center (News 12)
 
 
- – May 26, 2026 – The US carried out more strikes against Iran, just hours after negotiators arrived in Qatar to discuss ending the war. Central Command claimed the strikes, which targeted missile sites near a major port and naval base on the Gulf Coast, were defensive. Additional strikes were conducted just two days later.
 
 
- – May 26, 2026 – The Trump-endorsed, scandal-ridden, and far-right candidate Ken Paxton handily defeated Senator John Cornyn, previously the second-highest-ranking Senate Republican, in a runoff. Cornyn had previously criticized the Capitol riot and argued that Trump shouldn’t run for reelection. During Trump’s first term, Cornyn had also criticized Trump’s firing of James Comey and defended figures such as Robert Mueller and Mark Esper against Trump’s attacks.
 
 
- – May 26, 2026 – In a possible violation of the First Amendment, the Trump administration proposed expansive nondisclosure agreements for all federal workers. The new rule would go beyond typical agency NDAs by prohibiting workers from sharing “non-public, confidential, or proprietary information,” thereby cracking down on whistleblowers. “Such broad gag orders would leave the public in the dark about how the government works, preventing the kind of informed debate that is critical to democratic accountability. The government can’t shroud itself in secrecy in a democracy,” said Esha Bhandari, director of the ACLU’s Speech, Privacy and Technology Project.
 
 
- – May 26, 2026 – After a physical at Walter Reed, Trump said he was in good health. “Everything checked out PERFECTLY,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. Since taking office, Trump has been observed with bruises on his hands, swelling in his legs, and a rash on his neck. He has also fallen asleep during official White House events.
 
 
 Trump Falls Asleep During White House Meeting (Libre News)
 
 
- – May 26, 2026 – Construction of a temporary cage-fighting arena for the UFC Freedom 250 fight began on the White House’s South Lawn, which is better known for hosting Easter egg rolls and Marine One departures. The UFC is run by Trump ally Dana White, and the fight will commemorate both the country’s independence and Trump’s eightieth birthday.
 
 
- – May 26, 2026 – Interior Secretary Doug Burgum suggested without evidence that other countries were to blame for ongoing data center protests in the US. “Any place that’s trying to build data centers is getting bombarded with foreign-directed propaganda to try to block these from being built. This is just another attack on the US and our ability to be competitive,” said Burgum, echoing comments made by Kevin O’Leary, in which the Shark Tank billionaire specifically blamed China for protests against his data center project in Utah. Americans overwhelmingly oppose the construction of data centers.
 
 
 Kevin O’Leary’s Data Center Would Be the Largest in the World (More Perfect Union)
 
 
- – May 26, 2026 – The Trump administration announced that Americans exposed to Ebola in the Congo would be sent to Kenya rather than home for treatment. Public health advocates and Ebola experts criticized the move, arguing that the US already has specialized treatment centers and experience safely transporting Ebola patients from abroad and treating them; some critics even questioned whether the decision was based on politics, not medicine. “This is a disappointing abdication of what we owe our own citizens, particularly when they need us most,” said Dr. Craig Spencer, an Ebola survivor.
 
 
- – May 27, 2026 – During a Cabinet meeting, Trump said that if Iran didn’t agree to his terms, he would “blow them up.” When asked about Americans’ financial difficulties due to the war in Iran, he added, “I don’t care about the midterms.”
 
 
- – May 27, 2026 – Katie Miller, the wife of White House advisor Stephen Miller, doxxed Paulina Mangubat, the DNC’s deputy chief mobilizer. After Stephen Miller falsely claimed on X that Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico was transgender, Mangubat replied, “Shut up, you ugly fuck,” from the Democratic Party’s official account. In response, Katie Miller posted a picture of Mangubat. Describing Mangubat as “30, unmarried with no kids,” Miller wrote, “This is what a sad, unhappy, female Liberal looks like. It’s why Pew reports 50% of them have been diagnosed with a mental condition.”
 
 
- – May 27, 2026 – An AP investigation concluded that ICE detainees were dying by suicide at an unprecedented rate. At least ten detainees have died by suicide since Trump took office again, including seven since October, at a pace that far exceeded the detainee population growth. In comparison, zero to one detainees die by suicide in a typical year. Of the ten who died, nine were Hispanic men, and seven had no violent crime record. Most were in ICE custody for less than a month, some only for a few days. The AP revealed that many ICE detention centers did not uphold ICE’s standards, including those for medical and mental health screenings.
 
 
- – May 27, 2026 – The US military struck another alleged drug-smuggling boat in the eastern Pacific, killing two.
 
 
- – May 27, 2026 – The Justice Department opened a criminal investigation into the writer E. Jean Carroll, who successfully sued Trump for sexual assault and defamation. In 2023, Trump was found liable for sexually assaulting Carroll in the ’90s and for defamatory comments he made on social media in 2022 denying Carroll’s claims. In 2024, he was again found liable for defamation, this time for comments he made in 2019 alleging that Carroll was making up the assault to sell a book. 
 
 
- – May 28, 2026 – White House advisor Peter Navarro intervened in a $620 million deal with Vulcan Elements, a company linked to Donald Trump Jr.’s venture capital firm, ProPublica revealed. Three months before the Pentagon deal was announced, Trump Jr.’s firm took an undisclosed stake in the company, and both Trump Jr. and the Pentagon said Trump Jr. was not involved. However, interviews and records showed that Navarro, a friend of Trump Jr.’s, initiated the deal. “The call came from the White House: We have to get this done,” said an anonymous Pentagon official. After the deal, Vulcan’s valuation skyrocketed.
 
 
- – May 28, 2026 – NOTUS reported that Philip Alito, the son of Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito, was appointed to a job in the Treasury Department last year, a potential conflict of interest given Trump’s numerous legal cases before the court. “There’s no doubt he got the position because of who he is,” said a former government official. The younger Alito was working at the Treasury when a lawsuit against the department challenging Trump’s emergency powers appeared before the Supreme Court. The Treasury did not disclose the younger Alito’s status in court documents, and Samuel Alito did not recuse himself from the case.
 
 
- – May 28, 2026 – In mid-April, the Interior Department spent $5 million coating DC horse statues in gold, per a NOTUS report. The spending was part of $95 million in taxpayer funds spent on DC beautification projects ahead of the country’s 250th anniversary. Many of the contracts were awarded without full competition or transparency.
 
 
- – May 28, 2026 – The Pentagon announced a $9.7 billion contract with Dell that could financially benefit Trump personally, setting up a potential conflict of interest. On February 10, Trump acquired between $1-5 million in Dell stock. He then encouraged supporters to “go out and buy a Dell computer” at a Georgia rally, purchased additional Dell stock the following month, and praised Dell at numerous public events, including a White House Rose Garden lunch. The company’s founder, Michael Dell, sits on Trump’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, has appeared at White House events, and has pledged $6 billion to fund the administration’s “Trump accounts” project.
 
 
- – May 28, 2026 – The Treasury prepared to put Trump’s face on a $250 bill. A living person hasn’t appeared on US currency since 1866, and the practice is currently illegal. Last month, the Trump administration announced that Trump’s portrait and signature would also be added to certain US passports.
 
 
 Bessent Teases $250 bill with Trump’s Image, if Congress Approves (NBC News)
 
 
- – May 29, 2026 – Multiple artists announced they were dropping out of the Trump-affiliated Freedom 250 concerts, including Bret Michaels, Martina McBride, and Young MC. Days later, Trump said he would headline the event himself, then quickly reversed course and called for the concerts to be canceled. “We should have a giant MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN RALLY, for 250, instead of having overpriced singers, who nobody wants to hear, whose music is boring, and yet who do nothing but complain,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
 
 
- – May 29, 2026 – A federal judge ruled that Trump’s name must come down from the Kennedy Center and also blocked the administration from closing the Center for renovations. “The Kennedy Center’s organic statute makes it crystal clear that the Center is to be named for President Kennedy, and it cannot bear any other formal name or public memorial based on the Board’s unilateral say-so,” wrote Judge Christopher Cooper. In response, Trump threw a fit on Truth Social.
 
 
- – May 29, 2026 – Memos showed the Pentagon was recruiting junior-level troops to watch the UFC fights on the White House lawn. The troops were required to pay for their own travel and meet certain height and weight requirements. Back in October, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth criticized “fat troops” and troops with “unacceptable” physical appearances.
 
 
- – May 29, 2026 – The White House unveiled aliens.gov, a space-themed website comparing immigrants to extraterrestrials. The new website bragged that ICE had arrested almost half a million people in nearly 12,000 cities, including over seven hundred US citizens. In more than a fifth of the locations where someone was arrested, no criminal charges were filed. Additionally, the website listed Puerto Rico as a foreign country and included an “encounters” tracker linked to false data. WIRED reported that the website, in playing The X Files’ theme song from an apparently ripped CD, likely also violated copyright.
 
 
- – May 29, 2026 – Trump purchased stock in UFC’s parent company, TKO Group Holdings, while promoting UFC’s upcoming fight at the White House, according to a Huffington Post review of Trump’s financial disclosures. “Using the White House to promote a company whose stock you bought while promoting it is one of the worst conflicts of interest you could imagine,” said Jordan Libowitz, vice president of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington.
 
 
- – May 30, 2026 – The US military struck another alleged drug-smuggling boat in the eastern Pacific, killing three.
 
 
- – May 31, 2026 – The death toll from the Trump administration’s military campaign against suspected drug traffickers off the coast of South America surpassed two hundred people after more than sixty strikes. Days earlier, The New York Times reported that researchers had found no evidence the campaign had significantly reduced the availability of cocaine in the United States, despite nearly $5 billion in military spending and nearly nine months of operations.

articles.name: DPP readiness: When and how brands and suppliers can get started
articles.author: Simone Preuss
articles.full_text:
DPP readiness: When and how brands and suppliers can get started
The Digital Product Passport (DPP), part of the EU’s Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (ESPR), will create a standardised system for sharing comprehensive product data, from information about durability and recyclability to recycled content and environmental footprint.
“It is emerging as one of the most transformative regulatory and business shifts the fashion industry has faced in decades,” agree global trend forecaster Future Snoops (formerly Fashion Snoops) and enterprise SaaS (Software as a Service) platform GreenStitch in their joint report “Digital Product Passports: Designing for Future Regulation, Now.”
“While many organisations still see DPPs primarily as a compliance or IT initiative, the reality is far broader: DPPs will fundamentally reshape how products are designed, sourced, manufactured, marketed, sold, repaired, resold and valued across their entire lifecycle,” they emphasise.
The clock until implementation is ticking
Given that textile products placed on the EU market will require standardised digital product records linked to physical products only from mid to end 2029, many brands are under the impression that they still have time. But this is a misconception. “This is no longer a future watch item and action is required now. Brands should assume that DPP readiness will require robust product data, better design, upstream supplier engagement and efficient digital infrastructure able to support traceability, product transparency and lifecycle information at scale. In most cases, this will take 18-24 months to establish at scale.”
”The brands that win will be the ones that build for both compliance and commercial value from day one.“
In addition, the EU’s anti-greenwashing regulation (Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition, ECGT) is coming into force from September 2026, requiring brands to provide product-level data that is credible, structured, traceable and defensible. “Companies that wait until the 2028 Delegated Act risk entering the compliance window with fragmented data, disconnected systems, inefficient operations and significant compliance exposure,” warn Future Snoops and GreenStitch.
Three strategic directions
Growth, design decisions and digitalisation are the strategic perspectives to act on now. DPPs can create the digital product infrastructure needed to power resale, repair, authentication, customer engagement, warranty services, smarter product development and stronger sustainability claims, thus providing growth, efficiency and competitive edge. “The brands that win will be the ones that build for both compliance and commercial value from day one,” predict the organisations.
Some of the most critical drivers of DPP success are product design decisions as they determine material choices, fibre blends, trims, chemical treatments, construction methods and repairability. Thus, up to 80 percent of a product’s future compliance, circularity and commercial value is determined at the design st age.
Lastly, a company’s ability to digitise will determine how fast it can scale. DPPs will create massive data complexity across the fashion value chain, making manual management impossible. “Success will depend on software platforms, systems integration, automation and AI to manage and scale hundreds of product-level data points across materials, chemicals, suppliers, manufacturing, logistics and end-of-life pathways,” caution the report authors.
How can brands get started?
Future Snoops and GreenStitch recommend a five-step approach to DPP readiness. First, there needs to be a cross-functional DPP transformation team including design, sourcing, sustainability, IT, legal, finance, operations and marketing. The team should undertake a readiness gap assessment and audit all active sustainability marketing claims ahead of the ECGT directive enforcement in September. Unsubstantiated claims should be removed.
Second, brands should approach DPP design with business value in mind, not just compliance alone. “Build DPP use cases for resale, repair, authentication, aftercare and consumer engagement from the outset. Integrate DPP data requirements into new product development from the design stage, adding scoring tools to material and product approval processes,” advises the report.
Third, Tier 1, 2 and 3 supplier onboarding should start immediately. This includes assessing supplier data readiness early on, given that upstream traceability and data capture will be one of the most time-consuming elements of implementation. “Fabric mills, dye houses and material suppliers will likely create a big dat a bottleneck,” cautions the report.
The fourth step is to build the digital backbone, which includes a revision of existing systems like product lifecycle management (PLM), enterprise resource planning (ERP), lifecycle analysis (LCA) and traceability. This should identify any gaps in interoperability, data quality and scalability. “Prioritise digitalisation, system integration, automation and AI-enabled workflows to efficiently manage data,” advise Future Snoops and GreenStitch.
Last is the pilot phase, which is also a chance to learn and ultimately scale. Future Snoops and GreenStitch recommend to launch three to five product pilots in 2026 and 2027 to test data flows, technology integration, supplier readiness and consumer engagement. A roadmap covering governance, systems, process changes, AI enablement and readiness milestones will help, as well as monitoring evolving DPP technical standards to refine implementation plans as requirements are confirmed.
What kind of data will be required?
While the details for DPP data fields are still being worked out, core performance indicators or so-called design options (DOs) have emerged: The robustness score (DO1) assesses physical robustness of a garment after washing while the recyclability score (DO2) looks at blend composition and construction, both on a scale of 1 to 10. DO3, recycled content, determines the percentage of recycled fibre by mass and distinguishes between open-loop and closed-loop sources. DO4 looks at the carbon/environmental footprint of manufacturing (Tier 1– 3), likely including greenhouse gas emissions/carbon, energy, water and water pollution. Tier 4 will be likely excluded from Phase 1.
Other areas include substances of concern (SoC) like hazardous chemicals, microfibre risk with an initial qualitative classification and a potential move toward quantitative shedding metrics at a later point, supply chain traceability with mandatory Tier 1 facility identifiers and Tier 2-targeted, fibre composition and care, use and end-of-life guidance with contact details and instructions for repair services voluntary in this phase.
The advanced phase with a broader environmental and social data scope will start in 2033, requiring primary product specific LCA and full Tier-2 traceability. Social and due diligence fields are expected to enter the scope, as well as a quantitative microfibre shedding rate. The full circular phase will start from 2036 and be operational across the EU with real-time lifecycle tracking, cross-border data exchange and secondary data markets.
“A digital product passport is not just a compliance checkbox, it is the infrastructure for trust. When a brand can show, at the SKU level, exactly where a fibre came from, what its carbon footprint is, and how it should be handled at end-of-life , that product becomes legible to every stakeholder in the value chain. The brands that start building this data foundation today will already be ahead when DPP becomes a law within the next two to three years,“ sums up GreenStitch CEO Narendra Makwana.
How will consumers engage?
Current research, for example by Certilogo, shows that almost half (49 percent) of consumers are very or somewhat familiar with DPPs, more than previously thought. Transparency is the most appreciated benefit, with close to three fourths of consumers (71 percent) believing that DPPs will increase their trust in brands. “This trust comes from data, not claims, as consumers grow tired of green terms and far-reaching goals that amount to little,” states the report.
According to research by Authentique, a majority (90 percent) of consumers especially looks for material and composition, driven by both health and environmental considerations, followed by a certificate of authenticity (87 percent) from brands in view of counterfeiting concerns, especially when it comes to luxury products. Aftercare and repair instructions are third most likely to be used by consumers seeking to extend the lifetime of prized possessions.
Resale is perhaps “the most interesting element of DPPs for consumers” according to the report as 82 percent of consumers are looking to access product details and original imagery via DPPs. This aligns with data from Vogue Business according to which more than half (56 percent) of consumers would be more likely to purchase second hand items when a DPP is available. Warranty, sustainability data and rewards is also information that consumers would likely look for.
In terms of technical aspects, consumers are used to scanning QR codes, not only for fashion items. According to research by QR code management and marketing platform QRCodeChimp, close to half (44.6 percent) of global internet users scan at least one QR code per month and almost two thirds (64 percent) of shoppers have scanned a product QR code in-store. However, doing so requires a smartphone, internet access and digit al literacy to navigate QR inter face s and interpret data. “Elderly populations, lower-income consumers and those in digitally underserved regions lack one or more of these prerequisites. These communities are often the most impacted by fast fashion,” cautions the report.
Who has successfully implemented the DPP?
Brand case study: Nobody’s Child
London-based womenswear brand Nobody’s Child started in 2015 with the aim of improving its impact through design. More than half (51.4 percent) of all garments are designed with monomaterial fabrics and all styles are designed to be worn and re-worn. The brand’s partnership with the Reskinned platform facilitates easier recycling and resale.
DPP piloting began in 2023 with 25 products initially; currently, the DPP has been implemented on more than 1,500 stock keeping units (SKUs). Full collection implementation is planned for fall/winter 2025. The B Corp certified brand is currently working towards Tier 4 traceability across all collections, while finding ways to use DPP insights beyond compliance.
“Getting to where we are today hasn’t alway s been straightfor ward... [but]our approach remains the same as our overarching sustainability strategy: progress over perfection,” comments sustainability lead Philippa Grogan.
Among the brand’s key learnings is that good data and a strong, harmonised data architecture will create a solid foundation while supporting suppliers throughout the transition is also essential to success, as well as a cross-functional DPP task force, early adoption and scaling beyond pilots.
Supplier case study: Sutlej Textiles & Industries Ltd.
As one of India's largest integrated textile manufacturers, Sutlej Textiles & Industries Ltd. produces a wide range of spun yarns and fabrics for global brands across the UK, Europe and beyond. The company was committed to sustainability but lacked verifiable product data to proof it, hence decided on implementing the DPP for 75 yarn and fabric products through a hybrid approach: While GreenStitch enabled LCA methodology, DPP creation and regulator y tracking, Sutlej's own systems provided the manufacturing data backbone. It took just one month from kick-off to 75-product DPP coverage. Looking ahead, Sutlej plans to expand from gate-to-gate to cradle-to-gate LCA, broaden product category coverage and deepen supplier traceability.
“A Digital Product Passport is not a compliance document but a commercial argument. When environmental data sits next to price and lead time, sustainability stops being a cost and becomes your competitive advantage, ” states Sutlej CEO Ashish Kumar in the report.
A key recommendation for anyone starting out is to fix the data first before building passports as the DPP is only as reliable as its underlying data infrastructure. Another learning is to view the DPP as an analytical engine that provides operational insight, not just transparency. As seen on the brand’s side as well, ownership across departments and functions is key. In addition, sector-specific expertise matters as generic ESG platforms cannot replicate the process-level understanding that textile-specialist partners bring to the table. Last but not least, data reluctance is a trust problem, not a capability problem. Phased onboarding and clear data-use agreements can increase supplier engagement.
OR CONTINUE WITH

articles.name: Why enterprises need to rethink data in the AI era
articles.author: Korbinian Zollner
articles.full_text:
Why enterprises need to rethink data in the AI era
AI demands decentralised, governed, cost-efficient data architectures
Enterprises built their early AI strategies in a world that assumed relative freedom of data movement. That world no longer exists, so how do they adjust to the new world?
While it’s a cliché that data is the new oil, the truth is that data does need to be able to flow around an organisation and come to rest in some central location, where it can be refined to extract insight and value.
In recent years, that refining has come, of course, via AI.
Director, Solutions Architecture at Starburst.
But if we really think that analogy through, it also captures some of the problems enterprises currently face managing data.
Recently, the world has seen what happens when the free flow of oil, gas, and other fundamental resources is disrupted. Governments and companies are scrambling to work around supply chain interruptions in the short term and looking for energy sovereignty and resilience in the long term. In this case, centralization has become a liability, thanks to a single, but critical, chokepoint.
In the same way, the upheaval created by AI, paired with governments’ and regulators’ attempts to manage its impact, means companies need to rethink how they architect and manage their data. The difference is that the ways traditional data flows around organizations are changing.
After all, a centralized approach made sense when moving data was straightforward. Now, however, governance and sovereignty concerns and data movement costs have changed the calculus.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
AI transformation
AI alone has transformed the equation when it comes to the volume of data that must be managed. It’s not just training models that require massive amounts of data. Those models need constant updating and tuning with fresh data. And, if those models are to deliver value to the business, companies will be constantly running inference, which requires more data, and generates more data.
Unsurprisingly, governments and regulators have an interest in AI governance. This includes existing concerns about data residency and the possibility of new problems, such as data leakage into LLMs.
In Europe, for example, the regulatory landscape laid out by the GDPR mandate has been complicated by the rollout of the EU AI Act, which comes fully into force from August this year. In the US, companies face multiple federal and state-level regulations. Any, or all, of these could come into play as data is moved to that central refinery.
Governments also have an understandable strategic interest in developing sovereign AI, further complicating matters when it comes to both data and the models that work on it.
Once we consider this, it’s clear that only a few organizations are architected to handle the sheer scale of data involved in AI, and the governance it requires.
Companies grow messily, whether organically or through M&A, inheriting different infrastructures – and different governance regimes - as they sprawl across borders.
Data in the old world
In the old world, free-flowing data might have been seen as efficient. Now, given the vast amount of data involved, generating copies of data and moving data across borders is both fraught with risk from a governance perspective. And with escalating cloud egress fees, data movement becomes extremely expensive. At the same time, moving or copying on-prem presents both a financial challenge, and imposes a burden on already stretched technology teams.
What are our options in this new world? Few technology leaders have the option of simply opting out of the whole AI revolution. Whatever your personal views on the technology, few C-suites are prepared to sidestep the AI race.
But we can lay out a roadmap for how to manage data – and compute – in this new world.
To start with, we need to understand the environment we’re really operating in. This may well include accepting that a hybrid or multi-cloud architecture is going to be the normal state of affairs. The very nature of AI, with companies needing to access multiple models and multiple services, means that traditional monolithic, central approaches simply won’t scale.
This, in turn, means every technology leader needs to be crystal clear on what governance means for their organisation and its data, whether that’s data privacy or residency requirements. And it’s imperative that governance is embedded in the AI workflow from the outset. It’s too important to be an afterthought or kicked down the road as other priorities arise.
What this makes clear is that it will normally make more sense to bring compute and those critical AI models to the data, not the other way round.
This isn’t just about reducing data movement costs or producing multiple copies of data. It’s about reducing the friction that comes with reconciling governance requirements as data moves around organizations and across borders. But it can also mean reduced latency and fresher data, making AI more effective.
That’s not to say that it’s not sometimes necessary to move data. But if that’s the case, let’s be mindful and deliberate about it.
But while data becomes increasingly decentralized, it’s imperative that we centralize the management of data access and build the platform accordingly. This lays the groundwork for clear data governance and sovereign AI alike.
By rethinking how they manage data movement, technology leaders can bypass the escalating egress costs and compliance traps embedded in the old way of doing things. The result is an AI strategy that is both scalable and sustainable, enabling enterprise-grade AI, wherever their data lives.

articles.name: Inside Nasdaq CFO Sarah Youngwood’s AI playbook
articles.author: Sheryl Estrada
articles.full_text:
Sarah Youngwood has a ranking system for artificial intelligence—and it has nothing to do with algorithms. Inside Nasdaq’s finance function, employees now earn belts for AI proficiency the way martial artists do: white belts for foundational knowledge, advancing through levels that require hands-on delivery and the ability to teach others. Youngwood has mandated that everyone on the finance team reach at least white belt. Her long-term goal is for 20% of the team to reach black belt status.
The belt system is one window into how Youngwood, EVP and CFO of Nasdaq, is approaching what she calls an embedded capability—not a standalone initiative. AI, in her view, should be reshaping everything: market infrastructure, internal finance operations, workforce culture.
 
“If we are Nasdaq, it is our role to lead the charge,” she told Fortune earlier this month from her 26th-floor corner office above Times Square. “To show what AI can do and how we can become an AI-first finance function.”
AI will be incredibly powerful for forecasting in finance, Youngwood said. By combining macro assumptions, pipeline data, and leadership actions, it enables better real-time decision-making—the core goal of any finance function, she explained. Its impact spans everything from cash allocation to invoice processing and beyond. Governance and human oversight are essential to the process, she said.
Youngwood joined Nasdaq as CFO in 2023 after spending more than two decades at JPMorgan Chase in roles including CFO of its consumer and community banking business, head of investor relations, and CFO of global technology. She also served as CFO of UBS Group. That background left her with a simple conviction about technology investment: prove the return. “Finance is in charge of a great deal of corporate data,” she said. “And AI is all about the data.”
The stakes are real. Nasdaq landed at No. 470 on the Fortune 500 this year, returning to the ranking five years after its 2021 debut. Today, the company centers its strategy on three pillars—architecting modern markets, powering the innovation economy, and building trust across the financial system—and Youngwood argues AI sits at the core of all three. Once known primarily as a stock exchange, Nasdaq has evolved into a large-scale software and technology provider for the financial industry, with roughly 10,000 employees worldwide and about half in product and technology.
“We are the trusted fabric of the financial system,” Youngwood said. Where we apply AI is in everything we do.”
Measuring what matters
Despite the rapid pace of AI adoption, Youngwood applies a familiar financial lens to technology investment: return on invested capital.
The measurement framework works in three stages. First, Nasdaq looks at employee engagement: are people completing AI training and actually using the tools? Next comes velocity: is AI improving throughput, accelerating workflows, or enabling faster development cycles? Only then does the company measure financial impact—what those gains translate to in revenue growth, cost efficiency, or productivity.
That discipline extends to how Nasdaq allocates capital across time horizons. The company categorizes investments into “horizon zero”—foundational needs like cybersecurity—followed by short-term return initiatives, medium-term bets, and longer-term R&D. Youngwood uses the same framework to evaluate AI spending, treating it not as a separate budget category but as a lens applied across the whole portfolio.
That foundation required years of groundwork. Over the past two years, Nasdaq has focused on standardizing data definitions, centralizing information, and building dashboards capable of supporting more advanced AI applications. “You need your data in tip-top shape,” Youngwood said. “Once you have that, you’re prepared for generative AI.”
Investments Nasdaq made a decade ago in cloud infrastructure and early AI capabilities now underpin its positioning in generative AI. “We couldn’t see the whole map at the time,” Youngwood noted. “But those small investments gave us the foundation to be very well positioned today.”
AI everywhere—inside and out
Youngwood uses AI across her function for everything from administrative tasks to forecasting and financial planning, with more advanced initiatives integrating AI into core systems and workflows. She has also made sure her top technology leaders sit at the same table as the finance team—a deliberate signal of how tightly finance and tech are now linked.
The same logic applies externally. “What we’re doing with AI is putting it everywhere—in every process for our clients and for ourselves,” Youngwood said. One example: Nasdaq Verafin’s Agentic AI Workforce platform, launched last year, is now used by 650 financial institutions. Youngwood points to ease of implementation as a key factor in its adoption.
The broader context makes the stakes clear. On June 12, SpaceX went public on Nasdaq, marking the largest IPO in history. The milestone arrived as debate grows over whether AI will disrupt traditional software business models. Nasdaq CEO Adena Friedman has argued the opposite—that AI will accelerate software innovation rather than replace it. Youngwood’s job is to make the financial case for that bet, determining how aggressively the company invests and shaping the investor narrative around the results.
As for her own “belt” journey, Youngwood gets no special treatment. She is going through the new process alongside her team and is on track to reach yellow belt next month, with plans to soon progress to green.
